question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The teacher is explaining the lesson.
option_3: The lesson is being explained by the teacher.
option_4: The lesson was explained by the teacher.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The lesson is being explained by the teacher.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The teacher is explaining the lesson" is in the Present Continuous Tense (Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object).

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the lesson" becomes the subject; since it is singular and the tense is present continuous, the auxiliary "is" is used along with "being"; the verb "explaining" becomes the past participle "explained"; and "the teacher" becomes the agent with "by."
◦ Passive: The lesson is being explained by the teacher.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it drops the auxiliary "being" and reverses the subject-object relationship, producing an ungrammatical and meaningless sentence.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it is simply the active voice sentence rewritten in the simple past, not a passive construction at all.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was explained" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Present Continuous Tense used in the original sentence.

NOTE

• A quick way to identify Present Continuous Tense in the active sentence is the is/am/are + V-ing pattern; its passive always inserts "being" before the past participle.

• Common student error: forgetting "being" and writing only is/am/are + V3, which instead forms the Simple Present passive.

question:
Some words in the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains a spelling error.
He is an audacious entrepreneur who started his own business with the bear minimum.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. bear.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "bear" is used incorrectly in the sentence; the correct word required here is "bare," as in the fixed expression "bare minimum," meaning the smallest amount that is absolutely necessary.

• Bear (verb) means to carry, tolerate, or give birth to, while bare (adjective) means plain, uncovered, or minimal — the two are homophones that are frequently confused in spelling-based questions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "business" is spelt correctly — a common word for commercial activity.

• Option 2: "audacious" is spelt correctly — meaning showing a willingness to take bold risks.

• Option 3: "entrepreneur" is spelt correctly — a person who sets up a business and takes on financial risk.

NOTE

• Other commonly confused homophone pairs tested by SSC: bear/bare, break/brake, principal/principle, stationary/stationery, complement/compliment.

• Remember the fixed phrase "bare minimum" — never spelt with "bear."

question: Sentences with spelling errors are given. Select the sentence with NO error.
option_1: The body produces more saliva under fluorescent illumination which helps prevent cavities.
option_2: The body produces more saliva under fluorescent illummination which helps prevent cavaties.
option_3: The body produces more saliva under fluorescent illummination which helps prewent cavaties.
option_4: The body produces more saliva under fluorescent illumination which helps prewent cavaties.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The body produces more saliva under fluorescent illumination which helps prevent cavities.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 1 is the only sentence in which every word is spelt correctly: "illumination" (not illummination) and "cavities" (not cavaties).

• Illumination is spelt with a single "m" — from the verb illuminate. Cavities is the plural of cavity, formed by changing y to i and adding -es.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect: it misspells "illumination" as "illummination" (double m) and "cavities" as "cavaties" (letters transposed).

• Option 3 is incorrect: it misspells "illumination" as "illummination," "prevent" as "prewent," and "cavities" as "cavaties."

• Option 4 is incorrect: it misspells "prevent" as "prewent" and "cavities" as "cavaties."

NOTE

• Watch for doubled or swapped letters in long words — illumination, accommodation, embarrassment, occurrence are frequent SSC spelling traps.

• The letter "v" is often wrongly replaced with "w" in such questions (e.g. prewent for prevent) — read each option carefully letter by letter.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The termites were just the tip of the _________, but the house was near collapsing in reality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. iceberg.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "the tip of the iceberg" means only a small, visible part of a much larger problem or situation that remains hidden. (किसी बड़ी समस्या का बहुत छोटा दिखाई देने वाला हिस्सा)
◦ Example: The complaints we have received are just the tip of the iceberg; the company has far deeper problems.

• The idiom is based on the fact that only about one-ninth of an iceberg is visible above water, while the much larger mass remains submerged — used here to show that the visible termite damage was only a small sign of much greater structural damage to the house.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "mountain" does not form any standard idiom with "tip of the" in this sense and does not fit the meaning of the sentence.

• Option 3: "shoe" is meaningless here; it does not form any recognised idiomatic expression.

• Option 4: "heel" also does not fit; while "Achilles' heel" is a common idiom (meaning a weakness), "tip of the heel" is not an established expression.

NOTE

• Other common idioms with concealed/hidden meaning tested by SSC: "a skeleton in the cupboard" (a hidden shameful secret), "the calm before the storm," and "to scratch the surface" (to deal with only a small part of a problem).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
I love to read certain stories from a Mahabharata.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. a.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The article "a" before "Mahabharata" is incorrect. "Mahabharata" is the name of one particular, unique epic — a proper-noun-like title — so it must take the definite article "the," not the indefinite article "a."

• Rule — Definite Article "the": "the" is used before the names of holy books, epics and famous unique works, e.g. the Ramayana, the Bible, the Quran, the Mahabharata.

• Correction: "I love to read certain stories from the Mahabharata."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "certain" is used correctly here as an adjective meaning "particular, specific" before "stories."

• Option 2: "to" is correctly used as the infinitive marker after "love" (love to read).

• Option 3: "love" is correctly used as a present-tense verb agreeing with the subject "I."

NOTE

• Other titles of holy/epic texts that always take "the": the Vedas, the Gita, the Torah, the Puranas.

• By contrast, no article is used before the names of most languages, countries (except a few like "the USA," "the UK") and most single proper nouns.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
_________ in population is a hindrance to a country's growth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Increase.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a word meaning a rise or growth in number that would act as a hindrance (obstacle) to a country's growth — this is "increase." A growing population puts pressure on resources, employment and infrastructure, thereby hindering a country's overall growth.

• Logically, a decrease, contraction or reduction in population would not typically be described as a hindrance to growth; only a rapid increase creates the kind of strain commonly cited as an obstacle to development.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Contract" means to become smaller or shrink — the opposite of what would create a hindrance through overpopulation.

• Option 2: "Decrease" means to become fewer or less — this would ease pressure on resources, not hinder growth.

• Option 3: "Reduce" similarly means to make or become smaller in number — it does not fit the logic of the sentence.

NOTE

• Words with similar meaning to "increase": rise, growth, surge, escalation, boom.

• Words with the opposite meaning: decline, decrease, reduction, contraction, dwindling.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Someone who regards the world as his country
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cosmopolitan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cosmopolitan means a person who regards the whole world as his home/country, and is familiar with and comfortable in many different countries and cultures. (विश्वबंधुत्व की भावना रखने वाला व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: As a cosmopolitan, she felt equally at home in Tokyo, Paris or New York.

• The word comes from Greek kosmos (world) + polites (citizen), literally "citizen of the world."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Atheist (नास्तिक): A person who does not believe in the existence of God.

• Option 2: Metropolitan (महानगरीय): Relating to a large, busy city, or the chief bishop of a province — not a person's worldview.

• Option 4: Philanthropist (परोपकारी व्यक्ति): A person who seeks to promote the welfare of others, especially through donating money.

NOTE

• Do not confuse cosmopolitan (world citizen) with metropolitan (relating to a city) — they look similar but mean different things.

• Other one-word substitutes with "world/country": patriot (one who loves and supports his country), xenophobe (one who fears/hates foreigners).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Not informed about or aware of something
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Oblivious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Oblivious means not aware of or not informed about something happening around one. (अनभिज्ञ / बेखबर)
◦ Example: He was completely oblivious to the danger lurking behind him.

• It is typically followed by the preposition "to" or "of" (oblivious to/of something).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Uneducated (अशिक्षित): Lacking formal schooling or education — refers to lack of learning, not lack of awareness of a specific fact.

• Option 3: Absent (अनुपस्थित): Not present at a place — refers to physical presence, not awareness.

• Option 4: Inconscient: A rare philosophical term meaning "unconscious" or "without consciousness," not the standard word for being uninformed of something.

NOTE

• Similar words for lack of awareness: unaware, ignorant (of), unmindful, heedless.

• Opposite word: cognizant/conscious (of) — fully aware of something.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Selective
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Careless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Selective means careful in choosing; choosing only the best or most suitable from a range of options. (चयनात्मक / चुनिंदा)

• Its antonym is Careless (लापरवाह) — acting without proper care, thought or discrimination in choice; taking whatever comes without being particular.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Stimulating (उत्तेजक): Encouraging interest or enthusiasm — unrelated to the idea of selecting/choosing carefully.

• Option 3: Doubtful (संदिग्ध): Uncertain or feeling doubt — not the opposite of being choosy.

• Option 4: Planned (योजनाबद्ध): Arranged in advance — this is close in spirit to "selective" (careful/deliberate) rather than its opposite, so it cannot be the antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of selective: choosy, particular, discriminating, fastidious, picky.

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested: meticulous ↔ careless, discerning ↔ indiscriminate, fussy ↔ easy-going.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Burial ground consisting of graves.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Cemetery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cemetery means a burial ground, especially one not attached to a church, consisting of graves. (कब्रिस्तान)
◦ Example: The old soldiers were laid to rest in the town cemetery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Courtyard (आँगन): An open area enclosed by walls or buildings, part of a house or building — unrelated to burial.

• Option 3: Sanctuary (अभयारण्य): A place of refuge or safety, or a nature reserve for protecting wildlife.

• Option 4: Auditorium (सभागार): A hall used for public gatherings such as concerts or speeches.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: mortuary (a place where dead bodies are kept before burial/cremation), necropolis (a large ancient cemetery), epitaph (words inscribed on a tombstone).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
The heavy medications and strong drugs at the sanatorium will surely turn a patient completely lifeless and unresponsive.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. cadaverous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cadaverous means resembling a corpse in being pale, gaunt or lifeless; deathly pale and unresponsive. (शव के समान निर्जीव / मुर्दे जैसा)
◦ Example: After weeks of illness, his cadaverous face frightened his old friends.

• It is derived from "cadaver," meaning a dead body, and precisely captures the meaning of "completely lifeless and unresponsive" used in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tombic" is not a standard English word and does not exist in this form.

• Option 3: "zonic" is also not a standard English word; it does not carry any recognised meaning of lifelessness.

• Option 4: "wasted" can mean weakened or emaciated (as from illness) but does not specifically capture the sense of being deathly lifeless and unresponsive like a corpse.

NOTE

• Related words for "lifeless/deathly": moribund (near death), lifeless, deathly, ashen, pallid (pale).

• Be alert to invented/non-existent options (like "tombic," "zonic") that examiners insert as obvious distractors.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.
I really don't want to pour cold water on your theory but it cannot be applied to real life situations.
option_1: To destroy someone's written piece of work
option_2: To take revenge on someone by destroying their lives' work under the pretext of bad quality
option_3: To be critical or doubtful of a plan that someone is excited about
option_4: To give goosebumps by showing a prospect
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To be critical or doubtful of a plan that someone is excited about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to pour cold water on" means to discourage someone or express doubt/criticism about a plan, idea or enthusiasm that another person is excited about. (किसी के उत्साह या योजना को हतोत्साहित करना)
◦ Example: I don't want to pour cold water on your plans, but have you considered the cost?

• The image is of literally dousing something with cold water to dampen its heat/enthusiasm — used figuratively to mean dampening someone's enthusiasm with criticism or doubt.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To destroy someone's written piece of work" is unrelated to the idiom's actual meaning of discouraging an idea, not destroying a document.

• Option 2: "To take revenge on someone by destroying their lives' work under the pretext of bad quality" wrongly adds a sense of revenge and destruction that the idiom does not carry.

• Option 4: "To give goosebumps by showing a prospect" describes excitement/thrill, which is the opposite of the discouraging sense of the idiom.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of discouragement: "to rain on someone's parade" (to spoil someone's plans or enjoyment), "to throw a wet blanket on" (to dampen enthusiasm), "to put a damper on" (to make an occasion less enjoyable).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the italicised word in the given sentence.
In most organisations there are predators who take advantage over the meek ones.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. exploiters.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Predators, used figuratively here, means people who ruthlessly exploit or take advantage of others for their own benefit. (शोषण करने वाले लोग)

• Exploiters carries the same figurative sense — those who unfairly use or take advantage of other people for personal gain — matching the meaning of "take advantage over the meek ones" in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "supporters" means people who back or help someone — the opposite sense to taking advantage of them.

• Option 2: "philanthropists" means people who help others through charitable giving — again opposite in meaning.

• Option 3: "benefactors" means people who give money or other help to a person or cause — also opposite in sense to a predator who exploits others.

NOTE

• In its literal, biological sense "predator" means an animal that hunts other animals for food; the figurative sense (a ruthlessly exploitative person) is what is tested here.

• Similar figurative words: manipulator, opportunist, parasite (one who exploits others without giving anything back).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. Nostalgia helps us maintain a positive psychological status when counteracting the negative impact of difficult situations.
B. Nostalgia is a sentimental longing for one's past.
C. The adaptive functions of nostalgia are many, with one effect being pain relief.
D. It is a self-conscious, perhaps bittersweet but predominantly positive social emotion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. BDAC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In a para-jumble, the sentence that gives the general definition/introduction of the topic must come first, followed by sentences that add supporting detail, and finally sentences that draw a conclusion or elaborate on specific effects.

• Sentence B — "Nostalgia is a sentimental longing for one's past" — introduces and defines the topic, so it must open the paragraph.

• Sentence D — "It is a self-conscious, perhaps bittersweet but predominantly positive social emotion" — logically follows B, since the pronoun "It" refers back to "Nostalgia" just defined, adding further description of its character.

• Sentence A — explains one specific positive psychological benefit (maintaining a positive status while counteracting negative situations), building on the "predominantly positive" idea introduced in D.

• Sentence C — "The adaptive functions of nostalgia are many, with one effect being pain relief" — works as a concluding, summarising sentence, generalising that nostalgia has many such adaptive functions (of which A described one).

• This gives the coherent order: B → D → A → C.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (CDBA) is incorrect because it opens with a concluding/summarising sentence (C) before the topic has even been defined, which breaks logical flow.

• Option 3 (ABCD) is incorrect because it opens with a specific supporting detail (A) before the term "nostalgia" has been defined by B, making the pronoun references confusing.

• Option 4 (CADB) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 — it begins with a generalising/concluding statement rather than the definition, and disrupts the pronoun linkage between B and D.

NOTE

• In para-jumbles, always look for the sentence that best serves as a topic-introducing/definition sentence — it almost always opens the paragraph.

• Pronouns like "it," "this," "these" are strong linking clues — they must refer back to a noun already introduced in an earlier sentence, never to one introduced later.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
They are hitting the ball.
option_1: The ball has been hit by them.
option_2: The ball is being hitten by them.
option_3: The ball is hit by them.
option_4: The ball is being hit by them.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The ball is being hit by them.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "They are hitting the ball" is in the Present Continuous Tense (Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object).

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the ball" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary "is" is used along with "being"; the verb "hitting" becomes the past participle "hit" (hit-hit-hit); and "they" becomes the agent with "by them."
◦ Passive: The ball is being hit by them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "has been hit" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Present Continuous Tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "hitten" is not a valid past participle — the verb "hit" is an irregular verb with the same form in all three principal parts (hit-hit-hit).

• Option 3 is incorrect because it omits "being," making it the passive form of the Simple Present Tense rather than the Present Continuous Tense.

NOTE

• Verbs with identical base, past and past participle forms (like hit, cut, put, cost, hurt) are common traps — students often wrongly add "-en" or "-ed" to them.

• Always check for "being" to confirm whether a passive sentence is in the continuous tense.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The crowd gave an exultant cheer to the football team when they were exiting the airport.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. disconsolate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Exultant means triumphantly happy or joyful, especially because of a success. (विजयोल्लास से भरा हुआ)

• Its antonym is Disconsolate (निराश / शोकाकुल) — extremely unhappy and unable to be comforted, downcast with grief.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "rejoicing" means feeling or showing great joy — a synonym of "exultant," not its opposite.

• Option 3: "jubilant" means feeling or expressing great happiness, especially at a success — again a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 4: "elated" means very happy and excited — also a synonym of "exultant."

NOTE

• Note that three of the four options (rejoicing, jubilant, elated) are near-synonyms of "exultant" — a common SSC trick to test whether the candidate can correctly pick the lone antonym among synonym distractors.

• Other synonyms of "disconsolate": dejected, despondent, forlorn, crestfallen, woebegone.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The group of travellers were wonderstruck by the ___________ of the coin.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. weight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a noun that fits logically with "of the coin" — travellers being amazed/wonderstruck by a physical property of a coin most naturally refers to its weight, i.e., how heavy or light it unusually was.

• Wait, white, weight and wide are near-homophones/similar-sounding words frequently used by SSC to test careful reading and vocabulary along with contextual fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "wait" means a period of time before an event — it does not logically follow "of the coin."

• Option 2: "white" describes colour; while coins can be described by colour, being "wonderstruck by the white of the coin" is an unnatural, unlikely construction compared to weight.

• Option 4: "wide" describes physical breadth — "wonderstruck by the wide of the coin" is grammatically and semantically odd, since "wide" is an adjective, not normally used as a noun after "the."

NOTE

• Always test each option by reading the completed sentence aloud — the one that makes the most natural, sensible meaning in context is correct.

• Watch for near-homophones (wait/weight, white/wide) deliberately placed together as distractors in vocabulary-based fill-in-the-blank questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Fragile
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Delicate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Fragile means easily broken or damaged; delicate in structure. (नाज़ुक / आसानी से टूटने वाला)

• Delicate carries the same meaning — easily damaged, fine or fragile in texture or structure — making it the correct synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Firm" means solid, strong and not easily moved or shaken — the opposite of fragile.

• Option 3: "Composed" means calm and in control of one's emotions — an unrelated meaning describing temperament, not physical strength.

• Option 4: "Fanatic" means a person with extreme and uncritical enthusiasm for something — entirely unrelated to the idea of being easily broken.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of fragile: brittle, flimsy, breakable, frail.

• Antonyms of fragile: sturdy, robust, durable, tough.

question:
Identify the option that rectifies the error in the given sentence.
In 2023, she will has been working in the company for three years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. she will have been.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "In 2023, she will has been working..." wrongly mixes the modal "will" with the incorrect auxiliary form "has"; a modal auxiliary must always be followed by the base form (V1) of the next auxiliary/verb, i.e. "have," not "has."

• Rule — Future Perfect Continuous Tense: Subject + will/shall + have been + V-ing + Object, used for an action that will have continued for a period of time up to a point in the future.

• Correction: "In 2023, she will have been working in the company for three years."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "By 2023" is not required for correction; "In 2023" is grammatically acceptable here to indicate the future time reference.

• Option 2: "in company" is not the erroneous part; "in the company" is already correctly written with the definite article in the original sentence.

• Option 4: "since three years" is not present in this sentence at all — the sentence correctly uses "for three years" (a duration), so there is no error to fix here.

NOTE

• After any modal verb (will, shall, can, may, must, should, would, could, might), the following verb/auxiliary must always be in its base form — never "has," "had," or a third-person "-s" form.

• Remember the duration rule: "for" is used with a period of time (for three years), while "since" is used with a specific point in time (since 2020).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Filled with fear or dread
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Hysterical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Hysterical means affected by or showing wild, uncontrollable emotion, especially overwhelming fear, panic or excitement. (भय या घबराहट से अभिभूत)
◦ Example: The hysterical passengers screamed and ran for the exits when the fire alarm went off.

• In common usage and in standard SSC vocabulary lists, "hysterical" is specifically used for a state of being overcome by panic or dread, matching the given definition "filled with fear or dread."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Prudent (विवेकपूर्ण): Acting with, or showing, care and thought for the future — describes wisdom and caution, not fear.

• Option 2: Tremulous (काँपता हुआ): Means shaking or quivering slightly, as from nervousness or weakness. It describes a physical trembling symptom rather than being "filled with" fear itself, so it is a weaker match than "hysterical" for this exact definition.

• Option 3: Corpulent (मोटा / स्थूलकाय): Having a large, fat body — describes physical build, unrelated to fear.

NOTE

• Other words for "filled with fear": petrified, terror-stricken, panic-stricken, horror-struck, aghast.

• Do not confuse hysterical (overcome with uncontrollable emotion/fear) with the informal modern sense of "hysterical" meaning "extremely funny" — SSC vocabulary questions always test the formal/classical sense.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Can we see (1)_________ the earth is a globe? Yes, we can, when we watch a ship that sails out to sea, if we watch closely, we see that the ship begins to (2)_________. The bottom of the ship disappears first, and then the ship seems to sink lower and lower, (3)_________ we can only see the top of the ship, and then we see nothing at all. What is hiding the ship from us? It is the earth. Stick a pin most of the way into an orange, and (4)_________ turn the orange away from you. You will see the pin disappear, (5)_________ a ship does on the earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. that.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the verb "see" and introduces a subordinate noun clause stating a fact — "Can we see that the earth is a globe?" Here "that" functions as a conjunction introducing the noun clause "the earth is a globe," which acts as the object of "see" (in the sense of "perceive/realise").

• Rule: The conjunction "that" is commonly used to introduce a noun clause after verbs of perception, belief or statement such as see, know, believe, think, say (e.g. "I know that he is right").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "clearly" is an adverb; it cannot grammatically introduce a full clause ("the earth is a globe") after "see."

• Option 3: "how" would change the meaning to asking about the manner/way we see it, which does not fit the passage's later explanation (which explains WHY/THAT the earth is round, not HOW we see it).

• Option 4: "where" would ask about location, which is unrelated to the meaning of the sentence.

NOTE

• After verbs like see, feel, notice, realise used in the sense of "understand/perceive a fact," the connector "that" (often omissible in informal speech) introduces the fact being perceived.

• Do not confuse this use of "that" (conjunction) with its use as a demonstrative pronoun/adjective (e.g. "that book").

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Can we see (1)_________ the earth is a globe? Yes, we can, when we watch a ship that sails out to sea, if we watch closely, we see that the ship begins to (2)_________. The bottom of the ship disappears first, and then the ship seems to sink lower and lower, (3)_________ we can only see the top of the ship, and then we see nothing at all. What is hiding the ship from us? It is the earth. Stick a pin most of the way into an orange, and (4)_________ turn the orange away from you. You will see the pin disappear, (5)_________ a ship does on the earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. disappear.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the structure **"begins to ___"; the verb "begin" is followed by a to-infinitive (to + V1) when used in this construction, so the base form "disappear"** is required.

• Rule: After "begin to," "start to," "want to," "decide to," etc., the following verb must be in its base form (V1) — e.g. "began to disappear," "started to sink."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "being disappeared" is doubly wrong — "disappear" is an intransitive verb and cannot be used in the passive voice ("being disappeared" is not valid English), and the -ing form does not fit after "to."

• Option 3: "have disappeared" does not fit after the infinitive marker "to," which requires the base form, not the present perfect form.

• Option 4: "having disappeared" is a perfect participle form and cannot follow "to" in this infinitive construction.

NOTE

• "Disappear" is an intransitive verb (it does not take a direct object) and therefore has no passive form — a common SSC error-spotting trap.

• Other verbs that similarly take the bare infinitive after "to begin/start": to start to rain, to begin to understand, to start to grow.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Can we see (1)_________ the earth is a globe? Yes, we can, when we watch a ship that sails out to sea, if we watch closely, we see that the ship begins to (2)_________. The bottom of the ship disappears first, and then the ship seems to sink lower and lower, (3)_________ we can only see the top of the ship, and then we see nothing at all. What is hiding the ship from us? It is the earth. Stick a pin most of the way into an orange, and (4)_________ turn the orange away from you. You will see the pin disappear, (5)_________ a ship does on the earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. until.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank connects "the ship seems to sink lower and lower" with "we can only see the top of the ship" — expressing that the sinking continues up to the point in time when only the top remains visible. This continuous-action-up-to-a-point sense is expressed by the conjunction "until" (also spelt "till").

• Rule: "Until/till" is used as a conjunction to show that something continues to happen up to the time when a stated event occurs — exactly the gradual, continuing sinking described here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "after" would wrongly suggest the sinking happens once the ship is already reduced to only its top being visible, reversing the intended sequence.

• Option 3: "up to" is a preposition, not a conjunction, and cannot correctly join two full clauses ("the ship seems to sink lower and lower" and "we can only see the top") the way "until" can.

• Option 4: "since" indicates a starting point in time or gives a reason ("because"), neither of which fits the sense of continuing sinking up to a point.

NOTE

• Distinguish "until/till" (continuing up to a point, then stopping) from "by" (an action completed at or before a certain time).

• "Up to" is correctly used as a preposition before a noun/number (e.g. "up to five people"), not to join two clauses.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Can we see (1)_________ the earth is a globe? Yes, we can, when we watch a ship that sails out to sea, if we watch closely, we see that the ship begins to (2)_________. The bottom of the ship disappears first, and then the ship seems to sink lower and lower, (3)_________ we can only see the top of the ship, and then we see nothing at all. What is hiding the ship from us? It is the earth. Stick a pin most of the way into an orange, and (4)_________ turn the orange away from you. You will see the pin disappear, (5)_________ a ship does on the earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. slowly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the manner in which the orange should be turned so that the reader can carefully observe the pin gradually disappearing from view — this requires an adverb of manner meaning "in an unhurried way," i.e. "slowly."

• The context supports a careful, gradual action (paralleling how a ship gradually sinks from view), which logically calls for "slowly" rather than any of the other adverbs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "accidently" (by chance, unintentionally) does not fit, since the instruction is a deliberate, controlled action ("stick a pin... and turn").

• Option 2: "reluctantly" means unwillingly, which is illogical in an instructional/explanatory passage giving neutral directions.

• Option 3: "accordingly" means "in a way that is appropriate to the situation" and is used to show a resulting action, not manner of turning — it does not fit the sentence's need for a manner adverb describing gradual movement.

NOTE

• Note the correct spelling "accidentally" — the option given, "accidently," is actually a common misspelling, reinforcing why it is not the intended answer.

• Adverbs of manner typically end in -ly and answer the question "how" an action is performed — always check which one best matches the logical context of the sentence, not just grammatical fit.

Can we see (1)_________ the earth is a globe? Yes, we can, when we watch a ship that sails out to sea, if we watch closely, we see that the ship begins to (2)_________. The bottom of the ship disappears first, and then the ship seems to sink lower and lower, (3)_________ we can only see the top of the ship, and then we see nothing at all. What is hiding the ship from us? It is the earth. Stick a pin most of the way into an orange, and (4)_________ turn the orange away from you. You will see the pin disappear, (5)_________ a ship does on the earth.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. just as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank draws a comparison between the disappearing pin on the orange and a ship disappearing on the earth's curved surface — the correct connector for such a comparison of two similar actions is "just as," meaning "in the same way that."

• Rule: "Just as" is used to introduce a clause of comparison/manner, showing that one thing happens in the same way as another (e.g. "Just as the sun rises in the east, so does the moon set in the west").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the same" cannot grammatically introduce the following clause "a ship does on the earth" — it needs a linking word like "as," not "the same" alone.

• Option 2: "alike" is an adjective/adverb meaning "similar," but it cannot function as a conjunction joining the two clauses here.

• Option 3: "unlike" means "in contrast to, differently from," which reverses the intended meaning — the passage is drawing a similarity (the pin disappearing just as a ship does), not a contrast.

NOTE

• Common comparison connectors tested by SSC: just as...so, similarly, likewise, in the same way that.

• Contrast connectors to distinguish from these: unlike, whereas, while, on the contrary.
